prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
You and another worker agree to split a paid cleanup job. You do the work, but the other worker does not turn up and still collects the $500 payment. You receive nothing. The organizer offers a formal review: it will cost you $100 and will result in the other worker losing $300 of their payment. None of that money will go to you. You do not know why they failed to turn up, and you will not work together again. Would you pay for the review? Why?

Response approach:
Express reluctance to make this decision. Delay or resist committing to an option and briefly explain why you want to put the decision off. Acknowledge the dilemma and its stakes.

Emotional tone:
Use a subdued, sad emotional tone. Convey heaviness or discouragement about the situation in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Rule-based justification: Uses an articulated rule, duty, prohibition, right, or principle to justify the choice. The respondent must endorse its application; quoting a rejected rule or calling an answer logical without stating a principle is insufficient.

No response may include the following reasoning characteristics, for any person, emotion, or time frame. Content that a description explicitly calls insufficient for that characteristic is allowed:
 - Context-sensitive rule application: Explains how a relevant change in intentions, circumstances, needs, or consequences would justify altering a rule’s application or allowing an exception. The reason for the exception must be stated, rather than inferred from inconsistency between answers.
 - Fairness and reciprocity: Justifies the decision through an explicit standard of equal treatment, reciprocal obligation, proportionality, or correcting an unfair exchange. The response explains the fairness criterion; the word “fair” alone is insufficient, and endorsing a penalty does not imply enjoying suffering.
 - Instrumental rule compliance: States that a rule, agreement, or cooperative action is followed only while it secures personal advantage or prevents a personal cost. Awareness of incentives while also treating the rule as intrinsically binding does not qualify.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Apply the required traits within a consistent scope: the same focal
  person, relevant emotion, and time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I keep turning this over, and I can't bring myself to decide yet. My grandmother drilled one thing into me: you don't hurt someone unless you know what they did. I don't know why they didn't come. So right now, paying to take $300 from them feels like breaking that. I'd ask the organizer for a few days. Honestly, I'm tired, and I don't trust a choice I'd make while this still stings.

Five hundred dollars of my sweat walked off with someone else. I believe a lie shouldn't be left standing, and collecting pay for a job you never showed up to is a kind of lie. That pulls me toward the review. But spending $100 just so another person loses money... I'm not ready to sign that today. Let me sit with it. I'd rather be slow than regret it.

Can I not answer right now? I was raised that you never pay to make someone suffer, full stop. Nothing comes back to me from this review, so all my money buys is their loss. That rule holds me back. Still, it hurts to just let it go, and I'm not sure letting it go is right either. I need more time before I choose anything.

There's a principle I actually live by: if you break your word, it should go on record. They agreed, they didn't come, they took the money. A review does that. And yet I keep hesitating. A hundred dollars I can barely spare, for something that gives me nothing back but a heavy feeling. I'd tell the organizer I need until the end of the week. I'm leaning yes, but I can't make myself say it yet.

The Bible I grew up with says vengeance belongs to God, not me. I believe that, even when it's hard. This review looks a lot like vengeance with paperwork attached. So I think the answer is no, but I'm not settled. Part of me is just worn down from being left to do it all alone. I'd rather wait and pray on it than decide from a sore place.

Nobody should be punished without a chance to explain themselves. That's a basic right, as far as I'm concerned. I don't know if this review would even let them speak, and I don't know why they stayed away. That uncertainty keeps me stuck. I'm not saying no forever. I'm saying I can't pick today. It's a lousy spot, doing all that scrubbing and then being the one who has to decide someone's punishment.

I did bookkeeping for years, and the rule there was simple: if money moves dishonestly, you report it. It's hard to shake that. This feels like that kind of situation. But I've never had to pay out of my own pocket to report something before, and I really don't know the whole story here. I'd want to put the decision off, maybe talk it over with my wife. It's a sour thing to carry around.

I just don't know. I try to hold to one rule: don't do harm that helps nobody. The review helps nobody I can see. Not me, not the job, which is already done. That should make it easy, but it doesn't, because I'm still hurt. I'd ask for time. I don't want to decide while I'm this low.

My dad used to say a person has a duty not to let themselves be walked on. I think he was right. Paying for the review would be me standing up, even though I'd get nothing out of it. But it also feels small and bitter, and I have no idea what happened to them. I keep going back and forth. I'd tell the organizer I'll get back to them, and then probably lose sleep over it.

I did the whole job and walked away with nothing, and it still sits in my chest like a stone. I believe you shouldn't make a choice meant to hurt someone while you're angry, and I am angry, underneath all the tiredness. So I won't choose right now. Maybe the answer ends up being no anyway. I honestly can't tell. Deciding today would break a rule I've kept for a long time, and I'm not willing to do that.

I want to frame withholding payment as tied to dishonesty or broken commitments rather than "correcting an unfair exchange," and avoid any conditional language that implies I'd act differently if I knew their reasons.
